beats.headline: Does producer.send() actually send data?
beats.subline: Hint: It never touches the network directly.
beats.narration: Calling producer dot send looks like a simple RPC, but it's a lie. Your application thread never touches the network. It just drops bytes into a buffer and walks away.

beats.title: The Producer Pipeline
beats.subtitle: App Thread vs. Background Sender

nodes.label: Sender Thread
nodes.detail: Drains batches via NIO when full or timed out

beats.narration: Your thread serializes the record and appends it to the RecordAccumulator. A dedicated background thread then drains these batches to the broker using Java NIO. This decoupling is what makes Kafka fast.

beats.title: Batching Logic

steps.explanation: Wait 20ms to pack more records into one batch.

beats.narration: Don't leave linger ms at zero. By waiting a few milliseconds, you pack more records into a single batch, which drastically improves compression ratios and reduces broker CPU overhead.

beats.title: Latency vs. Throughput
beats.narration: You are trading a tiny bit of latency for massive throughput gains. For high-volume event streams, batching is not optional—it is required to keep the cluster healthy.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: linger.ms is your best friend for throughput

beats.narration: That's the pipeline. In Part 2, we break down why acks=all can still lose data if your broker settings are misconfigured.

beats.headline: Is acks=all actually safe?
beats.subline: Most teams get this wrong by ignoring the ISR.
beats.narration: Everyone says use acks=all for safety. But if your min.insync.replicas is set to one, you are one broker crash away from permanent data loss. Here is why.

beats.title: The Durability Gap
beats.subtitle: Why acks=all needs min.insync.replicas

nodes.label: Data Loss
nodes.detail: If min.insync=1, leader dies = data gone

beats.narration: Acks all only waits for the In-Sync Replicas. If your min insync replicas is one, the leader acknowledges the write even if it is the only one who has it. If that disk dies, your data is gone.

beats.title: Delivery Guarantees
beats.narration: For financial data, use idempotence and transactions. It prevents duplicates during retries and ensures atomic multi-topic writes. It is the gold standard for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines.

beats.title: Production-Grade Config
beats.caption: The 'Safe' defaults
beats.narration: Never rely on defaults. Explicitly set acks to all, idempotence to true, and ensure your topic has at least two in-sync replicas. Fail fast if these are misconfigured.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In

beats.narration: That's the durability layer. In Part 3, we look at the PID and sequence numbers that make idempotent producers possible.

beats.headline: How does Kafka stop duplicate retries?
beats.subline: It's not magic—it's a 64-bit ID and a sequence number.
beats.narration: If a network blip happens after the broker writes your data but before the ACK reaches you, your producer will retry. Without idempotence, you get a duplicate. Here is how Kafka prevents it.

beats.title: Idempotent Sequence Tracking
beats.subtitle: PID + Seq Number = Deduplication

nodes.label: Broker Check
nodes.detail: Discards if Seq exists for PID

beats.narration: The producer gets a unique PID on startup. Every batch gets a sequence number. The broker tracks these per PID. If it sees a sequence number it already committed, it discards the retry.

beats.title: Out of Order Protection
beats.narration: You can have five requests in flight for performance, but the broker enforces strict ordering. If batch two arrives before batch one, the broker rejects it until the gap is filled.

beats.title: Idempotence Scope
beats.narration: Remember, idempotence only works for the current session. If your app restarts, you get a new PID. Always build consumer-side deduplication if your business logic requires it.

beats.headline: Why is one partition always hot?
beats.subline: Default hashing is failing your high-volume tenants.
beats.narration: Default hashing works for most, but if you have a VIP tenant generating 40% of your traffic, they will crush one partition while others sit idle. Here is how to fix it.

beats.title: Custom Partitioner

steps.explanation: Isolate high-volume keys to a dedicated partition.

beats.narration: Implement the Partitioner interface to route specific keys to dedicated partitions. This prevents noisy neighbors from slowing down your critical traffic.

beats.title: Compression Codecs
beats.narration: Use Zstd for JSON logs. It gives you the best compression ratio with minimal CPU impact, saving you significant money on cross-AZ network traffic.
